frameworks.name: TEAM Partnership Acronym
frameworks.definition: A partner is worth adding only if they contribute at least one of four things: Time, Expertise, Assets, or Money that the founder genuinely lacks.

frameworks.name: C-L-O-S-E-R Sales Framework
frameworks.definition: A seven-step closing sequence: Clarify why they are here, Label them with a problem, Overview past experience and pain, Sell the vacation (outcome), make the Offer, handle concerns (Explain), Reinforce the decision after buying.

frameworks.name: Best-Case Worst-Case Close
frameworks.definition: A risk-reversal closing technique that explicitly names the best outcome (transformation) and worst outcome (work out for free and get refund) to eliminate perceived downside and accelerate commitment.

frameworks.name: Results Flywheel
frameworks.definition: A three-step self-reinforcing loop: acquire customers, get them results, use those results (proof) to acquire more customers.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi collected $4,972 in cash in his first month running his first gym in Huntington Beach, California (circa 2012-2013), which exactly matched his monthly rent of $4,972, driven primarily by a Facebook ad campaign he funded with roughly $1,000 from his remaining $6,000 in savings after spending $34,000 on build-out and $10,000 on a gym mastermind.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

numbers.axis: first-month cash collected vs. fixed overhead at launch

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that pre-selling memberships for three months before opening a brick-and-mortar location (collecting cash before costs begin) is structurally superior to opening first and marketing second, because all major costs (rent, staffing, build-out) start at opening day, so delaying opening while accumulating paying members maximizes cash-on-hand at launch.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Costs only begin when the location opens, so preselling creates a cash surplus that funds operations immediately rather than requiring the business to fight for survival from day one.
bounded_by: Does not apply if the founder does not intend to open a real location — taking money without intent to deliver is fraud

claims.text: Alex Hormozi used pre-sale ad spend across 5-10 markets (roughly $500-$1,000 per market) to identify lowest lead costs before signing a lease, treating the ad spend as market-selection insurance rather than lead generation. Markets with the lowest lead costs indicated better fit for expansion.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Running low-budget ads in multiple markets reveals demand elasticity before the business incurs any fixed cost commitment (lease, build-out), allowing selection of the highest-potential market rather than guessing.

numbers.axis: ad spend per market for pre-sale market testing

anchors.region: avoided lease cost if wrong market

bounded_by: Only works when the business has not yet committed to a lease in those markets

claims.text: Alex Hormozi's six-week challenge offer at his gym charged $500 upfront and then an additional $200-$300 in supplements 48 hours later, giving him $700-$800 in first-transaction revenue versus competitors who used free trials or $21-for-21-days offers that generated roughly $21 upfront and required three months to reach a single standard monthly membership equivalent ($99-$199/mo).
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Higher upfront cash allowed Hormozi to outspend competitors on advertising because his cost-to-acquire was immediately offset by first-transaction revenue, while competitors had to wait months for comparable cash.

numbers.axis: first-transaction revenue: challenge offer vs. free/low-barrier competitor offers

anchors.region: time for competitor to match Hormozi day-1 revenue

claims.text: Alex Hormozi's six-week win-your-money-back guarantee (lose 20 pounds or 10% of body weight in six weeks to get the $500 back) resulted in fewer than two refund requests on the unconditional guarantee over multiple years of operation, with approximately 80% of members hitting the weight-loss goal by the time Hormozi had refined operations versus 15% success rate in the first challenge cohort.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: The guarantee forced the team to improve accountability systems (public weigh-ins, meal plan adherence tracking) over time, which drove completion rates from 15% to ~80%.

numbers.axis: challenge completion rate by operational maturity

anchors.region: unconditional guarantee refund requests over years

bounded_by: The BMI-adjusted goal (10% of body weight for lighter members) was designed to prevent gaming but participants still gamed with water manipulation; Hormozi estimated a 5-6 pound give on both sides of official weigh-in

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that, for local gym-style businesses (circa 2012-2015), the gap between lead show rate (getting leads through the door) had more potential leverage than the gap between close rates because: converting 10% to 50% of leads to in-person appointments is a 5x improvement, whereas improving close rate from 50% to 80% is roughly a 60-70% improvement.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Show rate is a multiplicative upstream variable; any gains in show rate compound into all downstream conversion steps (close rate, upsells, LTV), whereas improving close rate only affects the final step.

numbers.axis: throughput multiplier: show rate improvement vs. close rate improvement

anchors.region: show rate improvement: 10% to 50% of leads

claims.text: Alex Hormozi observed that a business owner who employed one dedicated full-time lead-response caller (sole job: call every inbound lead immediately, 24/7) achieved 55% lead-to-close rate on 2-3 leads per day, compared to the industry norm of roughly 10% lead-to-close.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Calling a lead within 60 seconds produces a roughly 391% increase in conversion (approximately 5x); dedicating a single employee to this role eliminates the human tendency to defer calls due to competing priorities.

numbers.axis: lead-to-close rate by response speed and staffing model

anchors.region: cited uplift from calling within 60 seconds

bounded_by: Applies to businesses with low daily lead volume (2-3/day) where one caller is sufficient; high-volume businesses need scaled teams

claims.text: Alex Hormozi invested $250,000 in his second gym location (including a glass-feature wall that cost approximately the same as his entire first location build-out) and found it generated similar revenue to the first location, producing dramatically worse return on capital, because customers valued accountability, community, and trainer quality rather than premium equipment or aesthetics.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Founder assumed capital investment drove customer satisfaction, but customer jobs-to-be-done research revealed the actual drivers were intangible (accountability, community, belonging), making physical upgrades irrelevant to revenue.

numbers.axis: capex per location vs. revenue generated

claims.text: Alex Hormozi's rule of thumb for when to open a second business location: the first location must be growing without the founder's active involvement for six consecutive months before any energy is directed toward a second location.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.speaker_term: nail it before you scale it
claims.mechanism: Six months of owner-independent growth proves the system (not the founder) is generating results; scaling before this point multiplies the founder-dependency problem across locations.

numbers.axis: minimum autonomous growth window required before second location

anchors.value: 6 consecutive months of growth without founder

anchors.region: founder involvement required to pass threshold

bounded_by: Applies to brick-and-mortar and local service multi-location expansion; online or software businesses may have different natural forcing functions

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that brick-and-mortar businesses that scale privately (not via franchise) require a location-level profit-share operator model, where a dedicated operator receives a base salary plus a percentage of location profit, to create aligned skin-in-the-game incentives without giving away equity.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Profit-share structures make operators feel like owners without transferring equity; operators who share in location profit make decisions that improve margins rather than just following instructions.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi's recommended profit-share calculation for brick-and-mortar location operators: determine on-target earnings (OTE) for the skill level required, split 50% as fixed base salary and 50% as performance-based profit-share, with the profit-share percentage set so that median location performance delivers the variable half. If location outperforms, operator earns above OTE; if it underperforms, operator earns below OTE.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Splitting OTE 50/50 between base and variable pay ensures the operator is never fully insulated from location performance, creating financial incentives that align with owner interests on both upside and downside.

numbers.axis: illustrative profit-share structure on a $250K/yr location with $150K OTE operator

claims.text: Alex Hormozi contends that the worst partnership structure is two people with the same expertise forming a partnership because they are friends; all productive partnerships require at least one party to supply something the other genuinely cannot supply alone (Time, Expertise, Assets, or Money).
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: When partners share the same capability set, there is no complementarity; the partnership creates diluted ownership without proportional diluted risk, reducing return on equity for both parties.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that early equity is the most expensive equity, and founders should delay giving equity for as long as operationally possible; when equity must be given, the split should reflect who bears the most risk, not merely how many parties are involved.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Equity given early represents a claim on exponentially more future value than equity given later, because the business has not yet proven its value; risk is the appropriate weighting factor because the equity holder bearing the most risk should capture the most upside.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi found that forcing himself to generate creative variation in his gym ads every week (due to local market saturation) — producing 20-30 variations per week including seasonal re-framings like lean by Halloween, slim for Santa, and six-week transformation — built creative production capability that gave him an advantage when he later scaled nationally, where competitors produced only a few creatives per month.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: local market gym advertising with fast audience saturation
claims.mechanism: Local market audiences exhaust quickly, forcing high-frequency creative rotation; this forced volume builds creative intuition and speed that compounds into a structural advantage against competitors who had the luxury of slower creative cycles.

numbers.axis: ad creative production rate: local vs. national-level operators

anchors.region: Hormozi local gym (forced by market size)

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that discounting a core service offer is categorically wrong; the correct response to a discount request is to either add a bonus (same price, more value) or change the terms of the discount (e.g., require three referrals or public reviews in exchange for the price reduction) so the business receives equivalent economic value.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Pure discounts erode price integrity and signal low value; changing the terms of any discount converts a margin loss into an equivalent marketing asset (referrals, reviews, testimonials) whose value often exceeds the discount amount.
bounded_by: Applies to core service offers; lead magnets and front-end offers at discounted price are a separate category

claims.text: Alex Hormozi found that running internal promotions (themed add-on programs) to existing gym members four times per year — each generating $9,000 from 30 members paying $300 for a six-week add-on with 90-minute weekly sessions — effectively doubled the average micro-gym owner's take-home income, because the incremental revenue carries ~98% margins (only trainer cost is incremental; no customer acquisition cost).
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Internal promotions cost nothing to acquire (customer already exists) and little to deliver (one trainer session per week), so gross margin is near 100% on the variable cost basis; the average gym's thin overall margins (~12.5%) mean even modest incremental revenue has outsized take-home impact.

numbers.axis: internal promotion economics per quarterly run

anchors.region: average micro-gym annual take-home (industry stat cited)

bounded_by: Requires an existing paying customer base; does not apply to new/pre-launch businesses

claims.text: Alex Hormozi contends that selling zero-cost, zero-effort product upsells alongside a service — such as selling $200-$300 of supplements to each gym member — allows a business to entirely offset its advertising spend with upsell margin, making all service revenue net of acquisition cost.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: service business with physical product adjacency
claims.mechanism: If margin from the product upsell equals or exceeds total advertising spend, the advertising is effectively free; all service subscription revenue then becomes pure profit above fixed costs.

numbers.axis: supplement upsell revenue vs. advertising cost

anchors.value: sufficient to cover full monthly ad spend

anchors.region: effective ad cost after supplement margin

bounded_by: Requires a natural product adjacency to the service delivered

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that focusing on absolute dollars of profit (not ROAS or return-ratio) is the correct optimization target for ad spend; he observed a competitor spending $15,000/month at 4:1 ROAS and netting $45,000 while he spent $1,500/month at 10:1 ROAS and netted only $13,500 — a worse absolute outcome despite a better ratio.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: paid advertising for local or national service business
claims.mechanism: ROAS is a ratio that measures efficiency per dollar; total profit is a function of both efficiency and volume. Optimizing for ratio alone prevents scaling spend even when absolute returns would increase.

numbers.axis: absolute profit vs. ROAS at different spend levels

anchors.value: Hormozi 2.5x better ROAS but 3.3x worse absolute profit

bounded_by: Assumes ROAS does not drop below 1:1 at higher spend levels; the argument breaks down if increased spend produces negative returns

claims.text: Alex Hormozi contends that the founder identity must shift from being the best individual performer (closer, trainer, marketer) to being the best teacher of that skill to others, because individual performance caps at one person while teaching multiplies output across a team.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: any service business with a team
claims.mechanism: As long as the founder defines winning as personal performance, they will unconsciously hoard the skill (closing, training, ad management) because stepping back feels like losing. Redefining winning as teaching quality shifts that incentive, unlocking delegation.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that sales training should be compressed to the absolute minimum required for a new hire to close; his gym sales training was 1 hour 15 minutes covering seven steps and produced closers, in contrast to hundred-hour programs that add complexity without proportional close-rate improvement.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Fewer steps are easier to memorize and execute under pressure; each additional step multiplies failure points because a rep who forgets step 6 of a 7-step process is more likely to improvise badly than one who forgets step 40 of a 100-step process.

numbers.axis: sales training length vs. operational effectiveness

bounded_by: Applies to high-volume consumer service sales; complex B2B enterprise sales with long cycles may require deeper training

claims.text: Alex Hormozi found that collecting objections from prospects who did not buy and creating a single, high-quality templated solution for each objection (travel meal plan, budget grocery guide, home workout guide) converted objections into positive differentiators; once built, each bonus could be pre-loaded into a physical stack and deployed selectively in one-on-one sales conversations.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Creating a one-time templated solution to a recurring objection converts a per-sale friction into a permanently deployed asset; prospects perceive customization but the seller is executing at scale.
bounded_by: Less applicable to group or self-serve sales contexts where individual objection handling is not possible

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that authority and responsibility must be paired equally when delegating to operators; giving responsibility without authority produces paralysis (operator cannot act), while giving authority without responsibility produces misaligned power.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Misaligned authority-responsibility creates either operators who can be held accountable for outcomes they cannot influence (frustration, resignation) or operators who can act without accountability (waste, misalignment).

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that the biggest early lead-generation mistake is single-source dependency on a third-party platform (such as Groupon circa 2012-2015), because any platform can stop working overnight and a business with no alternative channel instantly loses its revenue engine.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Third-party platforms control the algorithm, pricing, and traffic; founders who do not own a direct-to-consumer acquisition channel are tenants who can be evicted.
bounded_by: Early-stage businesses may need to start with one channel; the risk increases as dependency deepens without building parallel channels

examples.text: At his first Huntington Beach gym, Alex Hormozi had no budget for staff or services, so he bartered gym memberships (a fixed-cost slot that cost him nothing marginal) for cleaning, personal training clients, food prep meals, and even laundry services. He got his first printer and scanner from an IT company owner in exchange for personal training sessions. His videographer for first ads was a small-time local videographer who could not afford a gym membership; Hormozi traded membership access for the video work, and those early ads performed well.

Alex Hormozi joined a gym mastermind before opening his first location (paying $10,000) and attended the first session without owning a gym. During a single day of conversations with 30-40 existing gym owners, he received advice on location selection, parking requirements, equipment brands to avoid, and layout ratios that he estimated saved him more than the $10,000 entrance fee on day one alone. He supplemented this by making weekend trips to shadow other gym owners, asking hundreds of questions about their operations.

Alex Hormozi was driving home for Christmas during the first year of his gym when he received a phone call from two former tanning-salon employees he had trained to sell his challenge. They reported that five people had signed up that day, with one paying in full and one on a split payment, generating $750 in same-day cash without him present. He pulled his car over, became emotional, and describes it as the first moment he understood the value of skill transfer over personal performance — a realization that shaped his subsequent focus on teaching rather than doing.

Alex Hormozi developed his travel meal plan bonus by listening to a single objection from a business professional who said she traveled frequently and was concerned she could not stick to the plan. He offered on the spot to create a travel meal plan specific to restaurant ordering; she agreed immediately. He then added that bonus to his permanent stack, and every subsequent prospect who raised travel as an objection received it as a prebuilt solution, converting a friction point into a differentiator at zero incremental cost.

Alex Hormozi filled his gym sales office walls with dollar-store framed before-and-after photos and screenshot reviews from Yelp and Google. When prospects expressed skepticism, he would point to the wall and ask: how much proof would you need? He would count photos one by one until the prospect told him to stop, then reframe the conversation: if this is enough proof, then what you're actually afraid of isn't whether we work. So what are you afraid of? This technique reliably surfaced the real objection (fear of embarrassment, failure, or looking stupid at the gym) so he could address it directly.

Alex Hormozi packed his gym to maximum capacity (40-50 people in 3,500 square feet across two simultaneous session types: strength and cardio). Rather than opening a second location or raising prices, he cut session times in half and consolidated to one session type. Approximately one-third of his customer base churned immediately because they disliked the change. He later recognized this as a mistake: the correct move was to leave the beloved product unchanged and either raise prices (to reduce demand to capacity) or open a second location.

Alex Hormozi had one personal training client at his Huntington Beach gym who paid approximately $4,000 per month for five sessions per week at 1.5-2 hours per session (~10 hours per week of guaranteed income). This unscalable revenue stream allowed him to reinvest all other gym cash flow into equipment, hiring, and expansion rather than covering personal living expenses. He fit the sessions midday between morning and evening group classes so they did not conflict with gym operations.

Alex Hormozi learned about absolute vs. relative return when a competitor moved into his local gym market and was spending $500 per day on ads (roughly $15,000/month) at a 4:1 ROAS, netting $45,000 per month. Hormozi was spending $50-$100 per day ($1,500/month) at a 10:1 ROAS and netting $13,500. He had been proud of his high ROAS; this comparison revealed he was optimizing a ratio while leaving $31,500 per month of attainable profit on the table.

Alex Hormozi's best gym manager — great at training, sales, and energy — was promoted to manager and excelled for six months. He then voluntarily asked to be demoted back to trainer, saying he would rather earn half as much and avoid management stress. Hormozi describes this as a turning point: he realized not everyone is motivated by money or advancement, and that building career paths and compensation structures requires understanding what each individual actually values rather than projecting the founder's own motivations.

practices.text: When you are poor and starting out, scan every line item in your expenses and proactively barter your service or inventory for anything you need — cleaning, printing, food, laundry — to preserve cash for revenue-generating activities.

Do not pretend to have resources or results you do not have when starting a business; admitting you need help makes people far more likely to assist you, especially other entrepreneurs who are one to two steps ahead.

When asking clients whether they followed a plan or protocol, do not accept binary yes/no answers; ask specific quantitative follow-up questions (e.g., how many days out of seven did you complete all three meals exactly to plan?) to surface actual adherence rates rather than perception-filtered answers.

In sales conversations, focus on the pain of the prospect's current situation and the vivid positive experience of the desired outcome; do not describe the steps required to get there (the process), as this creates objections rather than motivation.

When hiring an agency for a capability you lack, explicitly declare your intention to learn the skill so you can eventually replace them; negotiate an hourly teaching arrangement if the agency will not sell you learning access in their standard engagement.

Screenshot all five-star reviews from Google and Yelp, print them in dollar-store frames, and display them in your sales area to surround prospects with overwhelming social proof during the conversation.

Pair authority with responsibility equally when delegating to operators: explicitly grant a spending threshold (e.g., up to $1,000 or up to 100% of one month's customer spend) so the operator can resolve issues without calling you.

Run an internal promotional offer to your existing customer list approximately four times per year; pick one specific component of your service to feature as a standalone add-on program to generate near-100% margin incremental revenue.

When considering a product or service upsell, first ask whether it can be structured at zero additional time or labor cost; prioritize upsells that recover advertising cost so that service revenue operates above the customer acquisition cost.

Before asking whether your business can run without you, take a one-month vacation; what breaks reveals the true dependencies and provides a concrete checklist for the systems and people needed before scaling.
